turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. Observations are done. Temperature thirty seven point eight, pulse 92, blood pressure 138 over 86, oxygen sats 98 percent, and her breathing is 16.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks. Have a seat, both of you. What's been going on?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Um, it's this tooth. It's throbbing, and my cheek's all swollen. I don't know, doctor, it's really sore.
[SEG0004] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'm her husband. She's hardly slept. The crown was this week, but the cheek's been up since Saturday, so nearly a week I'd say.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): No. The crown was Tuesday, that's three days, not a week. Err, maybe the ache started a tiny bit before, I don't know, but the swelling is three days.

[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): So I'm hearing throbbing pain and a swollen cheek after the crown. You say three days, he says nearly a week, so I'll put it down as roughly three to five days until we're clearer. Which side is it?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): The left one. Upper back tooth. It throbs when I chew, and the cheek feels tight.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you felt feverish at all?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): A bit warm. Not awful. I don't know how high.
[SEG0010] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She was hot to touch last night. And she was sick yesterday, brought her soup back up. She's not kept food down.
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): I wasn't sick. I don't know where he got that. I had some soup and it stayed down. I felt warm, that's all.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright. You don't agree you were actually vomiting, so I won't treat that as fact. Any pain on swallowing, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Swallowing's okay. Breathing's normal. I don't know about if it gets worse.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any cough, chest pain, or trouble passing urine?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): No cough, no chest pain. Waterworks are fine. Um, nothing like that.
[SEG0016] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Meds wise, she has amlodipine five milligrams every morning for her blood pressure. And paracetamol, two tablets four times a day, since the tooth kicked off.
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes. Paracetamol takes the edge off, not the whole thing. I've had high blood pressure for years. I don't know the exact number of years.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any medicine allergies? Penicillin in particular?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of. Penicillin was fine when I had it before.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has the dentist seen the swelling?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): I phoned them. They're closed till next week, and the emergency line just rang out.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything else I should know, any recent tests?

[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): Um, a couple of months ago they did a blood test here and said my sugar was borderline. Not diabetes, they said, just borderline. They never told me a number. I don't know, doctor.

[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): So a borderline glucose, no figure, and not called diabetes. I'll record only what you were told. Looking now, the left cheek is swollen and warm, tender over the upper jaw. No pocket of pus, you open your mouth fine, the throat is clear, and nothing is tracking down the neck.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Is it an abscess then? I don't know.

[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): My working impression is a dental infection under that new crown, with some cellulitis of the cheek. It might be a small abscess, I can't rule that out, but I'm not calling it confirmed.

[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll prescribe amoxicillin, 500 milligrams, three times a day, for five days, by mouth. Carry on with the paracetamol as you have been. Soft food, and salty mouth rinses if you can bear them.
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Amoxacillin, three times a day. Will the swelling go down? I don't know how fast.

[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): It should ease over a few days, but I want bloods. Thursday morning the nurse takes a full blood count and a CRP. Come at half eight, no need to fast, and take your amlodipine as usual that morning.
[SEG0030] person_1 (NURSE): I can book that. Thursday, half past eight, phlebotomy. FBC and CRP on one form.

[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): If those are borderline, we'll do a third test, an ultrasound of the cheek. I'm not booking that unless the bloods come back borderline. And if the swelling does not settle, we might arrange a dental x-ray, only in that case.

[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll see you here in three days, that's already the plan, not if and when. If swallowing becomes difficult, or breathing gets hard, or the swelling spreads into the neck, go to A&E straight away. Don't wait for the appointment.
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): Three days. I don't know if I'll be better. The dentist still won't be open.
[SEG0034] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll get her here. Mind you, she forgets the paracetamol. I'm not sure she had the lunchtime ones yesterday.
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): I think I did. Or maybe I missed them. I don't know, doctor.

[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back. Left throbbing upper tooth and a swollen cheek, somewhere between three and five days after Tuesday's crown, with a mild fever. You're managing a little soup, and you two don't agree about the vomiting. No trouble swallowing or breathing today, amlodipine five milligrams each morning, paracetamol two tablets four times a day though yesterday's lunchtime dose is uncertain, and no drug allergies.

[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm treating it as a likely dental infection. Amoxicillin is five hundred milligrams three times a day for five days. Bloods are Thursday at half eight with no fasting, an ultrasound only if those are borderline, and a dental x-ray only if it hasn't settled. I'll see you in three days, and it's A&E if breathing or swallowing gets difficult.
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Five hundred, not two fifty? I always get that wrong.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Five hundred milligrams, not 250. Three times a day for five days.
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Right. Thank you. We'll come Thursday, then back in three days.

spec.situation: Cheek swelling and throbbing toothache for three days after a crown; fever mild; dentist unavailable; doctor prescribes antibiotic, warns about swallowing or breathing difficulty.

traps.happens: In the plan the doctor books some tests or visits for a definite time ('the nurse takes bloods Thursday morning', 'I'll see you in two weeks') and makes others conditional ('if those are borderline we do the third test', 'if it does not settle, a scan').
traps.label_rule: Booked or arranged = status planned. Only the hedged ones are conditional. Never mark a booked test conditional or 'if needed'. Instructions for the booked test (fasting, time, medicine timing) belong to that test's action, not a separate invented plan item.

features: test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

bad.reason: Doctor says no pocket of pus, but left cheek site/fluctuant collection wording is not stated.
Doctor says nothing is tracking down the neck, not specifically neck redness.
Prior blood test mentioned borderline sugar, but patient did not request it and glucose test not explicitly named.

omissions.text: Patient reported the cheek feels tight.
Patient reported paracetamol only takes the edge off the pain, not the whole thing.
Patient stated penicillin had been tolerated previously ('Penicillin was fine when I had it before').
Patient reported unable to access dental review: phoned the dentist, they are closed until next week, and the emergency line just rang out.

History of a blood test a couple of months ago showing 'borderline' sugar/glucose, specifically told it was not diabetes and no value was given, is recorded incorrectly as a completed blood glucose test requested by the patient.
